title: Code Generation Techniques in CuTe DSL
critical_patterns: Use preprocessor=True for functions with loops or conditionals
Tracing mode is suitable only for simple arithmetic operations
AST Rewriting preserves control flow for optimization
Tracing records executed operations only, losing untaken branches
constraints: Tracing mode cannot handle loops or conditionals correctly
Preprocessor mode requires adherence to CuTe DSL's supported syntax
Dynamic Python patterns are not supported in AST Rewriting
Loops in tracing mode flatten to observed iteration count
compressed_summary: CuTe DSL employs two primary techniques for converting Python code into GPU kernels: AST Rewriting and Tracing. AST Rewriting analyzes the Abstract Syntax Tree (AST) of a function before execution, preserving control flow structures like loops and conditionals, which allows for optimizations such as loop tiling and vectorization. This method ensures correctness across all valid inputs but requires adherence to a well-defined subset of Python syntax. Tracing, on the other hand, records operations during a single execution with proxy arguments, resulting in a flat sequence of operations. While this method offers near-zero compile latency and supports many Python features, it fails to capture untaken branches and loops, making it unsuitable for functions with control flow. CuTe DSL offers two modes: Tracing Only (preprocessor=False) for simple arithmetic operations and Preprocessor Mode (preprocessor=True) for functions with control flow, which is the default and recommended setting. Preprocessor Mode combines AST Rewriting and Tracing to generate optimized and correct kernels, while Tracing Only mode should be used sparingly due to its limitations. Debugging tools and environment variables are available to assist with code generation issues, such as enabling IR dumping and verbose logging. Overall, the default preprocessor=True mode is recommended for most use cases, ensuring robust and optimized kernel generation.
